title: The Accusative Case
sourceNote: The transcript is garbled; the rules, tables and the question words Wen/Was are clear. The example sentences are reconstructed from context and extended with extra examples.
objectives: I can explain what the accusative object is
I can ask Wen? and Was? to find the accusative object
I can use einen / eine / ein in the accusative
I can use den / die / das and keinen / keine / kein in the accusative

vocab.note: ich habe, du hast, er hat
ich esse, du isst, er isst

grammar.title: What is the accusative?
grammar.body:
Every sentence has a **subject** (nominative). Many sentences also have an **object**. This direct object is in the **accusative**.

The accusative object can be a person or a thing, singular or plural.

*Petra liebt Max.* Petra is the subject (nominative). Max is the object (accusative).
grammar.ar: الفاعل في حالة Nominativ، والمفعول به المباشر في حالة Akkusativ.

grammar.title: The questions Wen? and Was?
grammar.body:
To find the accusative object, ask a question:

- Object is a **person**: **Wen?** (whom?)
- Object is a **thing**: **Was?** (what?)

*Wen* is the accusative form of *wer*. *Was* does not change: it is the same in the nominative and the accusative.

examples.de: Wen liebt Petra? – Petra liebt Max.
examples.en: Whom does Petra love? – Petra loves Max.

examples.de: Was kauft er? – Er kauft einen Tisch.
examples.en: What does he buy? – He buys a table.

grammar.title: Indefinite articles: ein, eine
grammar.body: Only the **masculine** changes: **ein → einen**. Feminine (*eine*), neuter (*ein*) and plural (no article) stay the same as in the nominative.
grammar.ar: المذكر فقط يتغير: ein يصبح einen.

grammar.title: Definite articles: der, die, das
grammar.body:
Again only the **masculine** changes: **der → den**. *die*, *das* and plural *die* stay the same.

The accusative object can also stand at the beginning of the sentence. The verb is still in second position: *Den Apfel esse ich.*

examples.en: I eat the apple (the apple, that is what I eat).

grammar.title: Negative article: kein, keine
grammar.body: *kein* follows the pattern of *ein*. Masculine: **kein → keinen**. All the others stay the same.

examples.en: I do not have a brother.

grammar.title: Summary: only masculine changes
grammar.body: Remember one rule: if the accusative object is **masculine singular**, add **-en**: *der → den*, *ein → einen*, *kein → keinen*. Everything else is the same as the nominative.

pronunciation.tip: After *u* the *ch* is a rough sound in the throat, as in *Buch*.

lines.de: Ja, ich habe einen Bruder und eine Schwester.
lines.en: Yes, I have a brother and a sister.

tip: Learn nouns with their article. When you learn *der Tisch*, also say *Ich kaufe den Tisch* once.

items.q: ___ liebt Petra? – Petra liebt Max. (Wen / Was)
___ isst du? – Ich esse einen Apfel. (Wen / Was)
___ kennst du? – Ich kenne Anna. (Wen / Was)
___ kauft sie? – Sie kauft einen Tisch. (Wen / Was)
___ sucht er? – Er sucht das Buch. (Wen / Was)

summary: The subject is in the nominative; the direct object is in the accusative.
Ask **Wen?** for persons and **Was?** for things to find the accusative object.
Only the masculine changes: der → den, ein → einen, kein → keinen.
Feminine, neuter and plural articles are the same as in the nominative.
The accusative object can start the sentence, but the verb stays in second position.
